findings.paper_title: A Financial Framework for the 2027-32 Medium Term Financial Strategy Refresh
findings.headline: Council tax income represents 63% of corporate funding and growing; a freeze would cost £121.9m over five years (18% of current budget).
findings.detail: The council is almost entirely dependent on council tax and relies on taking the maximum 4.99% increase each year. If council tax were frozen for five years, projected income in 2031/32 would be £121.9m less than planning assumptions. The Government's funding settlement has already factored in these maximum increases, so not taking them results in a real-terms reduction in overall funding.
findings.matters: Revenue concentration risk: the council has minimal flexibility on council tax and cannot use it as a mitigating lever if other funding sources deteriorate; it is already assumed at maximum. Any resistance to council tax rises or economic slowdown in the tax base becomes an unmitigated budget pressure.
findings.figures: £435.9m council tax precept in 2026/27 (63% of corporate funding); Band D currently £1,903.86; freeze would reduce 2031/32 income by £121.9m
findings.quote: If council tax was frozen at the current 2026/27 Band D level over the next five years, projected council tax income in 2031/32 would be £121.9m less than current planning assumptions, representing 18% of the current 2026/27 net revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: A Financial Framework for the 2027-32 Medium Term Financial Strategy Refresh
findings.headline: The council has set planning assumptions for scenarios where savings delivery falls below 100%; historical delivery has been ~70% of target.
findings.detail: Scenario Risk 2 explicitly models 'delivery of Budget Reduction targets at same level as 2025/26 (circa 70%) or any % below 100%'. This is not presented as hypothetical; it is included as a plausible scenario for the MTFS, indicating the council expects savings delivery to fall short and is planning contingency for it.
findings.matters: Planning explicitly for 70% delivery of savings targets is an admission that achieving the full reduction is not certain; it signals that the council is managing against expected failure to deliver planned efficiencies.
findings.figures: Scenario assumes 70% delivery (based on 2025/26 outturn) versus 100% target
findings.quote: Scenario/Risk 2: 2026/27 delivery of Budget Reduction targets at same level as 2025/26 (circa 70%) or any % below 100%

findings.paper_title: A Financial Framework for the 2027-32 Medium Term Financial Strategy Refresh
findings.headline: Savings delivery is at risk; if 2026/27 overspends, required savings in 2027/28 will increase and reserves will deplete significantly.
findings.detail: The paper states: 'Any emerging overspend in 2026/27 is likely to increase the level of savings required in 2027/28 and future years, and significantly reduce reserves, unless mitigating action is taken.' The council is dependent on delivering £99.9m of savings over five years on top of managing current-year pressures; the framework identifies 'risks remain from rising demand increasing the costs of service delivery which may lead to in-year overspends and challenges delivering planned savings.'
findings.matters: This is explicitly flagging that the baseline assumption (current year holds, future savings are deliverable) is at risk; if 2026/27 overshoots, the council will have less cash buffer and higher required savings, creating a dual squeeze on the MTFS.
findings.figures: £99.9m savings required 2026/27–2030/31; 2026/27 Q1 monitoring expected in September will clarify position
findings.quote: Any emerging overspend in 2026/27 is likely to increase the level of savings required in 2027/28 and future years, and significantly reduce reserves, unless mitigating action is taken.

findings.paper_title: A Financial Framework for the 2027-32 Medium Term Financial Strategy Refresh
findings.headline: Pay inflation is already expected to exceed budget; the council has offered 3.3% but anticipates actual costs will be higher.
findings.detail: The council set aside 3.0% pay inflation in the 2026/27 budget and offered 3.3% to staff, but already estimates that 2026/27 pay inflation 'will exceed the 3.3% offered by the National Joint Council. Without any wider change to improve the Council's market position in terms of pay and reward, this cannot be contained.' This suggests the council is already facing cost pressures beyond budget in its largest controllable cost area.
findings.matters: Pay overrun is a leading indicator of budget control failure; if the council cannot contain labour costs (which represent a large portion of social care and other controllable spending), this signals either weak cost management or unmanageable service cost growth.
findings.figures: 3.0% provision in budget; 3.3% offered to staff; actual expected to exceed both
findings.quote: basic pay inflation in 2026/27 will exceed the 3.3% offered by the National Joint Council. Without any wider change to improve the Council's market position in terms of pay and reward, this cannot be contained within the 3.0% provision set aside in the 2026/27 MTFS

findings.paper_title: A Financial Framework for the 2027-32 Medium Term Financial Strategy Refresh
findings.headline: The DSG High Needs statutory override ends on 31 March 2028, at which point the council must find a sustainable solution for an accumulated cumulative deficit.
findings.detail: The council is currently using balance sheet resources to manage the cashflow impact of the DSG High Needs deficit while the statutory override is in place. The paper flags that a 'sustainable national solution' is needed after March 2028 but makes no assumption of what that will be; it is planning on the basis that the deficit will somehow be resolved. Until then, the council is using reserves to manage the deficit and is dependent on an unconfirmed High Needs Stability Grant.
findings.matters: A structural deficit in a ringfenced grant that sits outside the council's control, funded by drawing down general reserves until a government solution materialises, is a material off-balance-sheet liability for a lender assessing financial position.
findings.figures: Override expires 31 March 2028; cumulative deficits managed through balance sheet through that date
findings.quote: managing the cumulative DSG High Needs deficit position and responding to the prolonged budgetary and cashflow challenges arising from the growing cumulative deficit until the end of the Statutory Override on 31 March 2028.

findings.paper_title: A Financial Framework for the 2027-32 Medium Term Financial Strategy Refresh
findings.headline: The Department of Education has confirmed zero Basic Need grant funding for school places to 2027/28 with no indication of future funding.
findings.detail: The council has a statutory duty to provide school places but will not receive grant funding from central government. This means the council must either fund growth from its own budget, defer provision, or halt capital projects. The paper describes this as 'a step change' in capital pressures and signals that prioritisation will result in approval only for 'unavoidable' projects or those delivering 'greatest benefits'.
findings.matters: A statutory obligation with zero dedicated funding creates a structural budget pressure that will require either capital borrowing or diversion of other capital resources; for a lender, this signals ongoing pressure on the capital strategy and cash flow.
findings.figures: Zero funding confirmed to 2027/28; Department of Education has given no indication of future funding
findings.quote: the risk to the funding of the provision for new school places with the Department of Education having confirmed zero Basic Need grant funding for Warwickshire up to 2027/28 and no indication of funding in future years.

findings.paper_title: A Financial Framework for the 2027-32 Medium Term Financial Strategy Refresh
findings.headline: £6.2m of social care costs are not funded in the current budget and must be absorbed through contingency reserves.
findings.detail: Adults and Children's Social Care have £6.2m of unfunded pressures that were identified in the 2026/27 s.25 statement. The council plans to manage anything beyond this through spending controls and the Short-Term Financial Risk Reserve. However, initial forecasts suggest 2026/27 will see 'continuing, significant pressures' in these high-demand areas, which could exceed the contingency and force further savings in 2027/28.
findings.matters: Unfunded social care spending in the current year is a concrete budget leak; a lender evaluating the council's financial control would flag this as evidence of either unrealistic budgeting or cost growth the council cannot manage.
findings.figures: £6.2m unfunded; total 2026/27 budget £702.3m
findings.quote: £6.2m of pressures in children's and adult social care (as outlined in the 2026/27 s.25 statement accompanying the budget resolution) were not fully funded in the agreed budget and MTFS.

findings.paper_title: Appendix E - Reserves Schedule 2025-26
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation implementation reserve established at £11m
findings.detail: A new LGR Implementation Reserve was created with 11,000k allocation, moving from zero opening balance to 11,000k closing balance. The reserve name indicates the council is preparing for Local Government Reorganisation, though the specific scope, timeline and total expected costs are not detailed in this schedule.
findings.matters: Major local government restructuring creates transition risks and costs; lenders need visibility on the scope, timeline, financial impact and whether this is mandatory or discretionary reorganisation.
findings.figures: New reserve of 11,000k
findings.quote: LGR Implementation Reserve 0       11,000   11,000

findings.paper_title: Appendix E - Reserves Schedule 2025-26
findings.headline: School capital financing cost reserve tripled to £13m with £8.8m added in one year
findings.detail: The Short Term Capital Financing Cost – School Sufficiency reserve grew from 4,200k to 13,000k, with 8,800k added in the financial year. This represents significant acceleration in capital financing provision for schools, though the reserve name suggests these are short-term financing costs rather than capital values.
findings.matters: Growing school capital financing costs indicate increased capital commitments or deferred costs materializing, both of which affect future borrowing needs and budget priorities that lenders monitor.
findings.figures: 4,200k to 13,000k, increase of 8,800k
findings.quote: Short Term Capital Financing Cost – School Sufficiency 4,200       8,800   13,000

findings.paper_title: Appendix E - Reserves Schedule 2025-26
findings.headline: Short-term financial risk contingency reserve increased by £10m to £22.4m
findings.detail: The Short-Term Financial Risk Reserve increased from 12,394k to 22,408k, an increase of 10,014k in the year. The council notes that this reserve is "used to balance out service overspends and is not available for allocation", indicating it is held specifically for managing unexpected service pressures.
findings.matters: Significant increases in contingency reserves indicate the council anticipates financial pressures or service delivery risks; this scale of increase suggests the council is bracing for tighter financial conditions.
findings.figures: 12,394k (opening) to 22,408k (closing), increase of 10,014k
findings.quote: The short term financial risk reserve is a contingency fund used to balance out service overspends and is not available for allocation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix E - Reserves Schedule 2025-26
findings.headline: Funding volatility reserve fully depleted from £29m to £0.2m
findings.detail: The Funding Volatility Reserve was drawn down from 29,035k to zero during the year. Although small offsetting reserves total 234k, the Volatility Total moved from 29,488k to 234k. The council has exhausted its primary buffer for managing income fluctuations.
findings.matters: Volatility reserves allow councils to absorb unexpected income shocks; their exhaustion signals significantly reduced financial shock absorption capacity and leaves the council exposed to income variations.
findings.figures: Funding Volatility Reserve reduced by 29,035k; Volatility Total moved from 29,488k to 234k
findings.quote: Funding Volatility Reserve 29,035       (29,035)   0

findings.paper_title: Appendix E - Reserves Schedule 2025-26
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant statutory override deficit worsened by £72.4m to £150.3m
findings.detail: The DSG Statutory Override Reserve moved from an opening deficit of 77,912k to a closing deficit of 150,308k. The effect of outturn column shows the deficit worsened by 72,396k during the financial year. This reserve carries accumulated school funding deficits that the council must manage under statutory override provisions.
findings.matters: Growing statutory school deficits represent structural misalignment between schools spending and grant funding, reducing financial flexibility and indicating accumulating liabilities.
findings.figures: Opening balance (77,912k), closing balance (150,308k), in-year deterioration (72,396k)
findings.quote: DSG Statutory Override Reserve (77,912)         (72,396) (150,308)

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Commentary on Service Capital Outturn.docx
findings.headline: Capital programme heavily dependent on S106 developer contributions — timing risk across multiple schemes
findings.detail: Multiple major schemes explicitly state dependence on S106 funding timing. A452 Cycle Route reprofiled to match S106 availability. Lighthorne Heath also noted as S106-dependent. This creates delivery risk if development consents slow or are refused.
findings.matters: Capital delivery dependent on external funding stream; slowdown in development activity across Warwickshire would cascade into capital programme delays
findings.figures: A452 (£1.945m) and Lighthorne Heath (£15.829m) explicitly S106-dependent; possibly others in Annexes A-M
findings.quote: A452 Kenilworth to Leamington Cycle Route (£1.945m)- The forecast indicates spend in 2026-27 due to changes in construction programme and updates to land costs. The project is also dependent on the availability of S106 funding and hence the budget has been reprofiled to match the timing of funds.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Commentary on Service Capital Outturn.docx
findings.headline: Major education schemes heavily delayed: Lighthorne Heath (£15.8m) and Shottery (£14.4m) now 2026-27
findings.detail: Two of the largest primary school projects are now reprofiled to 2026-27, both driven by planning delays and S106 funding timing. Lighthorne Heath is explicitly dependent on when S106 money arrives. Shottery was delayed by extended developer land-transfer negotiations.
findings.matters: Large individual capital schemes at risk of further delay; shows vulnerability to planning and developer-contribution timing
findings.figures: Lighthorne Heath £15.829m; Shottery £14.367m; Watlings Meadows £7.170m
findings.quote: Lighthorne Heath Primary School (£15.829m) - Project delays due to ongoing wider development site discussions. Spending is phased to 2026/27. Project also dependant on timing of S106 funding.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Commentary on Service Capital Outturn.docx
findings.headline: Funding gap emerging: cannot start some schemes without identifying additional sources
findings.detail: A3400 Birmingham Road scheme (£1.394m) is stalled because costs have increased beyond approved budget. The council says funding source must be identified to cover the increase before works can start. Oak Wood Secondary may also require additional funding once Fire Engineering Strategy is complete.
findings.matters: Council unable to fund all planned capital from existing allocations; shows execution risk and potential for further delays or scope reduction
findings.quote: A3400 Birmingham Road Stratford Corridor Improvements (£1.394m) Higher costs expected to complete the work hence funding source must be identified to cover increased costs before starting the works.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Commentary on Service Capital Outturn.docx
findings.headline: Additional £0.777m needed for SEN provision — being covered via corporate borrowing
findings.detail: 16 SRP (Special Resourced Provision) projects overran approved budgets by £0.777m once construction completed and children using the facilities. Needs were higher than forecast and only emerged during operation. Council is funding the gap through corporate borrowing and SEND blockheader reallocation.
findings.matters: Signals emerging cost pressures in statutory SEN spend and the council using corporate borrowing to plug capital shortfalls
findings.figures: £0.777m total overrun; individuals: Nethersole CoE (£0.093m), North Leamington School feasibility (£0.059m), Glendale Infant (£0.018m), Nursery Hill (£0.023m), Birchwood Primary (£0.043m), Phase 1 Kingsway Nursery relocation (£0.371m)
findings.quote: The following table shows cost increase at Q4 on Education SRP schemes where further work was identified once the project was completed and started to be used. It is driven by needs of the children using the provision and the environment.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Commentary on Service Capital Outturn.docx
findings.headline: £7.1m SEN expansion frozen — no further S106 developer funding received
findings.detail: Evergreen Round Oak site expansion for special educational needs is on hold because S106 (developer contribution) funding has stopped flowing. This represents a committed capital programme the council cannot currently deliver, affecting vulnerable children.
findings.matters: Shows planning-to-funding misalignment; councils dependent on S106 for capital delivery are vulnerable if development activity slows
findings.quote: Evergreen-Expansion of Round Oak site (£7.111m) – The project currently on hold due to no further S106 being received.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - P12 25-26 Commentary on revenue outturn variances
findings.headline: Children's internal legal fees overspent £0.790m (up £0.725m on prior year) due to case volume and duration
findings.detail: Legal recharge for 2025-26 is £0.725m more than 2024-25, reflecting an ongoing increase in the number of cases and placements the service is dealing with. This is a pass-through cost that rises automatically with case demand and suggests the Children's service is handling materially more complex, contested cases.
findings.matters: Legal costs are a trailing indicator of case complexity and contested proceedings; a 48% year-on-year increase (£0.725m on baseline of ~£1.5m) suggests systemic increase in case difficulty or challenge.
findings.figures: £0.790m overspend (P10 £0.611m, Q3 £0.610m); £0.725m increase on 2024-25; Driven by increased numbers and duration of cases
findings.quote: Internal Legal Fees – These have been slowly rising during the year with a final overspend of £0.790m (P10 £0.611m, Q3 £0.610m) due to increased numbers and duration of cases. The legal recharge for 2025-26 is £0.725m more than in 2024-25. This increase reflects the ongoing increase in the number of cases and placements the service is dealing with.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - P12 25-26 Commentary on revenue outturn variances
findings.headline: Parent & Baby residential placements jumped unexpectedly to £0.929m overspend after MTFS savings were actioned
findings.detail: A MTFS budget saving had been actioned against Parent & Baby placements based on historical trend, but the service experienced a dramatic, unexpected increase in activity. Weekly costs rose 42% from £5,151 (2024-25) to £7,331 (2025-26), driven by higher-than-expected Children in Care who are pregnant and rapid cost escalation. The council had cut the budget in anticipation of lower demand, then saw demand spike.
findings.matters: Forecasting failure: the council removed a savings line expecting lower demand, then demand rose 42%. Signals poor forecast linkage between social care demand and maternity services.
findings.figures: £0.929m overspend (P10 £0.850m, Q3 £0.600m); Weekly cost rise: £5,151 → £7,331 (+42%); MTFS saving actioned against this budget before demand spike
findings.quote: This financial year has seen activity levels dramatically increase which was an unexpected upturn in trend based on previous years, (indeed, an MTFS budget saving was actioned against this budget in 2025-26). The final position is an overspend of £0.929m (P10 £0.850m, Q3 £0.600m) The main reason for the increase in activity is a higher-than-expected increase of Children in Care who are pregnant coupled with the weekly average costs increasing at a fast rate, rising from £5,666 at Q1, to £6,280 at Q2, to £6,910 at P10 to a final rate of £7,331 for 2025-26. In comparison the 2024-25 rate was £5,151 per week.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - P12 25-26 Commentary on revenue outturn variances
findings.headline: Warwickshire Property and Development Group £2.457m commercial shortfall covered from Commercial Risk Reserve
findings.detail: The commercial property vehicle missed its £2.741m net income target by £2.457m, requiring drawdown from the Commercial Risk Reserve. Council states 'future years' returns expected to replenish the reserve,' but no detail on how shortfall will be recovered or whether business plan assumptions need revision.
findings.matters: A material miss on commercial vehicle income (90% of target) signals either optimistic business planning or deteriorating property market conditions. Replenishment reliance is concerning if reserve depletion continues.
findings.figures: £2.457m shortfall (target £2.741m, achieved £0.284m); Covered from Commercial Risk Reserve; £0.300m Scape Dividend to partially replenish reserve
findings.quote: As planned, the shortfall from the Warwickshire Property and Development Group net income target (£2.457m) will be met from the Commercial Risk Reserve, with future years' returns expected to replenish the reserve. Performance of the property group will continue to be monitored against the approved business plan.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - P12 25-26 Commentary on revenue outturn variances
findings.headline: Treasury Management one-off £11.599m income windfall masking structural service pressures
findings.detail: Treasury income exceeded budget by £11.599m due to interest rates remaining higher than forecast. This is explicitly marked as one-off and not sustainable; medium-term forecasts assume rates will fall. Additionally, corporate provisions of £4.380m were used to cover overspends elsewhere. Together these £15.979m of one-off items mask the fact that underlying services are in structural deficit.
findings.matters: A one-off treasury windfall is being deployed as a critical mitigation for service overspends rather than addressing underlying demand-driven deficits in children's and adult social care. When rates normalise, this cushion disappears and the council's true financial position will be exposed.
findings.figures: £11.599m treasury income above budget (one-off); £4.380m corporate provisions used; £15.979m total one-off mitigations; Corporate Services underspend £16.859m (-37.6%) heavily driven by treasury gain
findings.quote: Treasury Management income forecast shows performance exceeding the budget for 2025-26 by £11.599m, which is a critical, one-off mitigation for the wider service pressures being experienced across the Council. Continued higher interest rates have remained in place for longer than anticipated although rates are now beginning to fall. Consequently, this additional income cannot be relied upon in future years as medium-term interest rate forecasts are anticipated to reduce and so is treated as one-off income above a prudent budgeted level which we believe is sustainable over the medium-term.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - P12 25-26 Commentary on revenue outturn variances
findings.headline: Disabilities supported living overspend £5.985m with 20% volume increase and reduced income recovery
findings.detail: Disabilities overspend £5.985m (5% above £109.4m budget), driven primarily by supported living for Learning Disabilities. Numbers of people drawing on support increased 20% against budget, with a 5% cost increase since April 2025. A single individual's income review correction reduced income by £0.357m. Uncollected care contributions written off (£0.225m) due to collection failure and legal approval.
findings.matters: Combination of volume overshoot (+20%) and income losses signals both care-demand underforecasting and collection weakness in what should be more predictable (residential) care contracts.
findings.figures: £5.985m overspend (5% above budget); 20% increase in people requiring support; 5% cost increase; £0.357m income correction for single individual; £0.225m written off uncollected contributions; £0.169m overspend on direct payments
findings.quote: The primary factor is an overspend on the £109.4m budget for packages of care, with the overspend for residents in supported living, many with night support, accounting for the full overspend, 96% of which relates to Learning Disabilities. Supported Living has seen a 5% increase in the cost of support since April 2025, along with a 20% increase in the number of people who draw on support compared to what was budgeted.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - P12 25-26 Commentary on revenue outturn variances
findings.headline: Mental Health supported living volume surged 36% with 8% cost inflation and rising case complexity
findings.detail: Mental Health overspend £1.843m (7% above budget) driven entirely by supported living. Volume of those requiring support increased 36% since start of year, with cost per unit rising 8% above inflation assumptions. Complexity is escalating: rising dual-diagnosis cases (mental illness + substance misuse), Korsakoff's syndrome, and early-onset dementia. A single recent transition costs £0.416m per annum.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted volume surge (+36%) combined with complexity-driven cost inflation suggests the council underestimated population needs or has poor forecasting. High-cost complex cases create budget volatility.
findings.figures: 36% increase in volume requiring support since start of year; 8% cost increase above inflation; £1.843m overspend (7% above budget); Single recent transition: £0.416m/annum
findings.quote: Within Supported Living there has been a 36% increase in those requiring support since the start of the financial year, alongside an 8% increase in the cost, above the level of inflation provided for. This is driven by an increasing number of high-cost, complex cases, including a recent transition costing £0.416m per annum. The rising complexity reflects a higher incidence of dual-diagnosis cases involving mental illness and substance misuse, alongside more individuals presenting with Korsakoff's syndrome and early-onset dementia.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - P12 25-26 Commentary on revenue outturn variances
findings.headline: DSG High Needs Block statutory education deficit of £74.548m, exceeding budgeted overspend by £13.227m
findings.detail: The council budgeted for a £61.322m High Needs Block (HNB) overspend but outturn was £74.548m. Primary drivers include Independent Special School placements (£5.911m overspend), Post-16 places (£3.140m overspend), and top-ups to special schools (£1.954m overspend). EHCP numbers rose 1,427 (21%) since January 2025, from 7,868 to 8,295. Government has committed to fund 90% via High Needs Stability Grant for 2025-26, but 2026-27 support uncertain.
findings.matters: This is a statutory funding block where the council cannot refuse placements; uncontrolled EHCP growth (21% in 8 months) creates unfunded liabilities. Dependency on government grant creates refinancing risk if support is withdrawn.
findings.figures: £74.548m HNB overspend; £61.322m budgeted overspend; £13.227m variance above budget; EHCP numbers 8,295 as of 20 April 2026 (up 1,427 since January 2025, +21%); ISP 58 placements above budget (+9.6%); Post-16 167 places above budget (+23.2%)
findings.quote: In order to give a realistic budget for managers to work with the HNB budget was set (and revised due to slight changes in the grant allocation) with an anticipated budgeted overspend of £61.322m. The HNB actual outturn position has exceeded this by a further overspend of £13.227m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - P12 25-26 Commentary on revenue outturn variances
findings.headline: Children's residential placements demand surge driving £10.146m overspend
findings.detail: Weekly residential placements increased 23.6% year-on-year to 6,153 weeks, equivalent to 118 children in care daily compared to 96 in 2024-25. Average weekly cost rose 7.5% to £6,871 per week (exceeding MTFS price assumptions), with 23 placements costing over £10,000/week. This is the single largest driver of Children & Families overspend.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted demand escalation in high-cost placements directly consumes council resources; a lender would assess whether this is manageable within medium-term plans or signals underlying safeguarding complexity the council cannot control.
findings.figures: 6,153 weeks (up from 4,977 in 2024-25, +23.6%); £6,871/week average (up from £6,393, +7.5%); 118 children daily equivalent; 23 placements at £10,000+/week; 5 placements would cost £1m+ annually
findings.quote: The number of residential weeks purchased this financial year has continuously risen with 6,153 weeks being the final figure...Compared to the 2024-25 figure of 4,977, this is an increase of 1,176 weeks / 23.6%. On top of this demand increase, the average weekly unit cost has now risen by 7.5% from £6,393 per week in 2024-25 to £6,871 for 2025-26; this is substantially more than the MTFS assumptions on price increases.

findings.paper_title: Financial Outturn Report 2025-26_v1
findings.headline: 2026-27 budget relies on conditional DfE High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of cumulative £161.5m DSG deficit; no plan if grant is refused or delayed
findings.detail: The approved 2026-27 budget assumes 90% of the £161.5m cumulative DSG deficit as at March 2026 will be funded via a High Needs Stability Grant from the Department for Education. This is conditional on DfE assessment and scrutiny of the council's SEND Reform Plan, which was due to be submitted in July 2026. No further support detail for 2027-28 deficits has been announced. If the grant is refused, reduced, or delayed, the council has no alternative funding source.
findings.matters: The 2026-27 financial plan is contingent on an approval from central government that has not yet been awarded. The council has no fallback position. A grant refusal or material reduction would force immediate budget cuts mid-year or emergency borrowing.
findings.figures: Assumed grant: 90% of £161.498m = ~£145m; depends on DfE approval of SEND Reform Plan
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget assumes that 90% of the cumulative DSG deficit as at March 2026 will be funded through this grant, subject to Department for Education assessment and scrutiny of the Council's SEND Reform Plan, which is due to be submitted in July 2026; the impact of this assumption in 2026-27 is reflected in the budget agreed by Council in February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Financial Outturn Report 2025-26_v1
findings.headline: Overall reserves depleting rapidly: fell £71m in one year to £83.4m and planned to fall a further £53.8m by end of MTFS period to £29.6m
findings.detail: Total reserves fell from £154.4m to £83.4m (down £71m or 46% in one year). Useable reserves will fall by a further £53.8m over the 2026-31 MTFS period, reaching £29.6m by 2031. This trajectory reflects persistent revenue overspends being funded from reserves. The Short-Term Financial Risk Reserve is being built up (now £22.4m) but other reserves are being depleted to manage in-year pressures.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion at this rate is unsustainable. Reserves that took years to build are being consumed in 1-2 years. Once exhausted, the council will lack buffer capacity for in-year shocks and will be forced into service cuts or hard borrowing decisions. The planned end position (£29.6m useable reserves) may be insufficient for a council of this complexity.
findings.figures: Reserves March 2025: £154.381m; March 2026: £83.414m (down £71m); planned by 2031: £29.644m (further down £53.8m)
findings.quote: The impact of the outturn on 31 March 2026 will be a decrease in the overall reserves held by the Council over the 2025-26 financial year of £70.967m, taking the total reserve balance from £154.381m to £83.414m. Reserves balances are planned to reduce by a further £53.769m by the end of the 2026-31 MTFS period

findings.paper_title: Financial Outturn Report 2025-26_v1
findings.headline: Home to School Transport overspent by £1.9m, with SEN transport accounting for £1.7m despite identified data cleansing savings
findings.detail: Home to School Transport overspent by £1.855m. The council identified and corrected 650 pupils where Education and Transport records did not align and duplicated records, yet SEN transport still overspent by £1.682m. Earlier forecasts had prudently allowed for additional costs from clearing the EHCP application backlog, but this timing slipped into 2026-27. The number of EHCPs issued has risen sharply — from 7,294 in January 2025 to 8,295 by April 2026 (21% increase in 15 months).
findings.matters: The 21% rise in EHCPs in 15 months signals accelerating special needs demand. Even after data cleansing, SEN transport overspent materially. The timing slip of EHCP processing impacts simply defers rather than solves the cost problem.
findings.figures: Total overspend £1.855m; SEN transport £1.682m; mainstream £0.162m; EHCPs 7,294 (Jan 2025) to 8,295 (April 2026) = 1,427 additional (21% increase)
findings.quote: The net service overspend of £2.869m is mainly driven by Home to School Transport, where the outturn overspend was £1.855m. This comprised £0.162m on mainstream transport, £1.682m on Special Educational Needs (SEN) transport and £0.011m on Children in Care transport. The number of EHCPs as at 9th February 2026 was 8,221, while the number of EHCPs as at 20th April 2026 was 8,295 a rise of 1,427 (21%) since January 2025.

findings.paper_title: Financial Outturn Report 2025-26_v1
findings.headline: Social Care & Support overspent by £7.9m driven by cost inflation and increasing volume and complexity of need
findings.detail: Social Care & Support directorate overspent by £7.868m (3.1% of budget) despite substantial additional budget allocations from Social Care Grant and the Adult Social Care levy. The overspend reflects increases in unit costs above budget assumptions, rising number of residents requiring support, and increased complexity of needs. Main pressures: Disabilities 25+ (£5.985m), Older People (£3.728m), and Mental Health (£1.843m).
findings.matters: Persistent overspends in adult social care despite additional resource allocation suggests either planning assumptions are structurally wrong, or underlying demand/cost drivers are beyond the council's control and require different solutions. This is a multi-year trend indicating unsustainable service economics.
findings.figures: Overspend £7.868m (3.1%); Disabilities 25+ £5.985m; Older People £3.728m; Mental Health £1.843m
findings.quote: The financial pressures on Social Care and Support experienced in recent years have continued into 2025-26 despite significant additional budget allocations, funded from Social Care Grant and the Adult Social Care levy. The overspend is due to increases in the unit cost of support above assumptions supporting the 2025-26 budget, an increase in the number of residents requiring support, and an increase in the complexity of their needs.

findings.paper_title: Financial Outturn Report 2025-26_v1
findings.headline: Children's residential placements overspent by £8.4m, with internal homes running at 66.8% occupancy against 75% breakeven, creating structural deficits
findings.detail: Children & Families directorate overspent by £9.822m (8.4% of budget). The primary driver is residential placements (£8.398m overspend), compounded by emergency placements for hard-to-place children and placement breakdowns. The council operates internal children's homes with 15 beds but achieved only 66.81% occupancy in the year (3,658 of 5,475 possible days), while 75% is the breakeven point, putting the homes £0.408m into deficit. This suggests both rising unit costs for placements and underutilisation of internal capacity.
findings.matters: A £8.4m overspend on a controllable service (residential placements) that continues to deteriorate is a material pressure. The low occupancy of internal homes against breakeven suggests structural inefficiency in service delivery. Market pressures for placement costs are showing no sign of abating.
findings.figures: Residential care overspend £8.398m; Children & Families directorate overspend £9.822m; internal homes occupancy 66.81% vs 75% breakeven; homes deficit £0.408m
findings.quote: This forecast overspend is primarily driven by, and related to, a deteriorating position in respect of children's residential placements, including extra care placements (using emergency placements for hard-to-place children, including placement breakdowns). For the financial year in total the number of days occupied was 3,658 out of 5,475 which represents an occupancy of 66.81% compared to the breakeven point of 75%. This puts the homes into a deficit position at outturn of £0.408m although this is an improvement on previous months

findings.paper_title: Financial Outturn Report 2025-26_v1
findings.headline: Underlying revenue position masks £14.3m directorate overspend; the reported £3.3m underspend depends entirely on one-off Treasury income
findings.detail: Directorates overspent by £14.263m, but the council reported a £3.329m underspend. This swing is entirely due to £11.260m of Treasury Management income beating budget (from higher interest rates) and £4.972m of corporate provisions being deployed. The council explicitly states that without these one-off mitigations it would have reported a net overspend. Treasury income should not be relied upon in future years as interest rates are expected to normalise.
findings.matters: The structural underlying position is negative. The reported outturn is not sustainable — it depends on temporary treasury tailwinds that cannot be counted on. Spending controls will have to continue into 2026-27 because underlying services are not operating within budget.
findings.figures: Directorate overspend £14.263m; Treasury income £11.260m above budget; corporate provisions used £4.972m; residual underspend £3.329m
findings.quote: This outcome results from the one-off savings generated through spending controls, stronger-than-expected Treasury Management returns from a prolonged period of higher interest rates, and an effective cash investment strategy; without these mitigations, the Council would have reported a net overspend position.

findings.paper_title: Financial Outturn Report 2025-26_v1
findings.headline: High Needs DSG deficit has nearly doubled in one year to £161.5m and is forecast to reach £327.9m by 2028
findings.detail: The cumulative High Needs Block deficit rose from £86.9m at end of 2024-25 to £161.5m at end of 2025-26, driven by £74.5m overspend in the year. Based on current growth trajectory it will reach £327.9m when the DSG Statutory Override ends on 31 March 2028. The deficit is held in a negative reserve under the statutory override arrangement, protecting the General Fund but creating £7.5m in annual financing costs, forecast to grow to £17.4m by 2028.
findings.matters: A structural deficit of this scale at end of override represents a cliff-edge funding risk unless the government's announced High Needs Stability Grant materialises. The growth trajectory shows the problem is accelerating, not stabilising.
findings.figures: £74.549m overspend in year; cumulative deficit £161.498m (was £86.949m); forecast £327.9m by 31 March 2028; financing costs £7.515m in 2025-26 forecast to reach £17.38m by 2028
findings.quote: The cumulative High Needs DSG deficit to 31 March 2025 was £86.949m. and, based on outturn position has increased to £161.498m as at 31 March 2026. Based on the current growth trajectory of the annual deficit, the cumulative High Needs deficit is currently forecast to reach £327.9m at the point the extended Statutory Override ends.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management and Investment Outturn Report 2026_v1
findings.headline: Treasury investment income of £11.4m versus £4.7m budget is being used to mitigate revenue budget pressures but is explicitly non-recurring and dependent on interest rates and cash levels.
findings.detail: Investment income exceeded budget by £6.7m (£11.4m actual vs £4.7m expected). The council's own paper states this surplus 'helps mitigate in-year revenue budget pressures' but is 'considered windfall in nature and cannot be consistently relied upon' because it is sensitive to interest rate movements and the level of cash balances held.
findings.matters: The council is using non-recurring treasury income to cover what appear to be structural revenue budget gaps. As interest rates fall (already down to 3.75%) and SEND deficits consume cash, this windfall support will disappear, potentially exposing underlying budget imbalance.
findings.figures: £11.4m actual investment income versus £4.7m budget, average yield 4.4% (down from 4.96% prior year), Bank of England rate 3.75%
findings.quote: The total income from treasury investments during the year amounted to £11.4m, compared to a budget of £4.7m. It is important to note that while the additional income helps mitigate in-year revenue budget pressures, it is considered windfall in nature and cannot be consistently relied upon. This income is influenced by the level of cash balances and is sensitive to interest rate fluctuations.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management and Investment Outturn Report 2026_v1
findings.headline: Council cash position is being reduced by cumulative SEND deficit funding, with future support dependent on conditional government grants.
findings.detail: The council has had to fund accumulated Dedicated Schools Grant (special education needs) overspend, which has reduced cash balances. A High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of the historic deficit is expected autumn 2026 but is subject to Department for Education approval of a SEND Reform Plan. Two further years of DSG deficits are expected; future support is only 'indicated' by government, not confirmed, with no certainty until the Statutory Override ceases in March 2028.
findings.matters: Statutory services deficits that rely on conditional external funding introduce risk to cash forecasting and borrowing profiles. If the grant is delayed or reduced, the council must cover the shortfall from reserves or borrowing.
findings.figures: Cumulative SEND deficit, High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of historic overspend to March 2026, 2 further years of accruing deficits, Statutory Override ends March 2028
findings.quote: Cash balances are reduced due to the impact of having to fund the cumulative SEND deficit however a High Needs Stability Grant, covering 90% of the historic Dedicated Schools Grant overspend to March 2026, is expected to be paid (subject to Department for Education approval of a local SEND Reform Plan) in autumn 2026. Alongside this grant 2 further years of accruing DSG deficits are expected and these cashflows will have significant impact on overall cash, although Government has indicated further support for these deficits will be made available through the High Needs Stability Grant when the Statutory Override ceases in March 2028.

findings.paper_title: Appendix E - Reserves Strategy 2026-31 (17.02.26)
findings.headline: Warwickshire is holding earmarked reserves to fund uncertain Local Government Reorganisation costs pending government decisions on unitary proposals.
findings.detail: The council has established an Earmarked Reserve (LGR Implementation) to fund the costs of creating unitary local government in Warwickshire, with implementation either as one new council or two new councils. The document states the reserve balance will be reviewed after government decisions to ensure it remains adequate for 'different scenarios', indicating that the scope and cost of implementation remains uncertain.
findings.matters: LGR will impose significant one-off costs with unknown quantum and timing. If government decisions reveal costs exceeding the reserve, the council may need to draw additional reserves or seek borrowing, materially affecting financial flexibility over the medium term.
findings.figures: Earmarked Reserves (LGR Implementation) included in total £208.4m; specific amount not stated
findings.quote: Balance to be reviewed following government decision on local proposals for Warwickshire to ensure reserve value remains adequate for different scenarios.

findings.paper_title: Appendix E - Reserves Strategy 2026-31 (17.02.26)
findings.headline: Warwickshire has a Dedicated Schools Grant deficit that cannot be immediately addressed due to a Statutory Override, with reserves designated to apply a High Needs Stability Grant when the override expires.
findings.detail: The council has recognised a DSG deficit in its accounts as at 31 March 2026. A Statutory Override currently prevents immediate application of the High Needs Stability Grant to extinguish this deficit. The council must hold this grant in reserve until the Statutory Override ceases to have effect, creating a contingent liability with uncertain timing of resolution.
findings.matters: A DSG deficit is a material liability to the council's balance sheet. The timing of when it must be addressed—when the Statutory Override expires—is uncertain, making it a contingent cash call that could affect financial resilience when it falls due.
findings.figures: High Needs Stability Grant amount not specified; total revenue reserves £208.4m at end of 2025/26; DSG deficit amount not stated
findings.quote: Where the Statutory Override prevents immediate application of the grant to the DSG deficit, the authority must: hold the grant in an appropriate reserve; and apply the grant only to reduce the DSG deficit recognised as at 31 March 2026 when the Statutory Override ceases to have effect.

findings.paper_title: Revised Treasury Management Strategy and Investment Strategy Report
findings.headline: Warwickshire Investment Fund reducing investment in final year due to deliverability constraints
findings.detail: The WIF strategy proposes reducing overall investment levels in 2026/27 (its final commitment year) to ensure the level of planned activity is deliverable and within acceptable risk levels. The council is reviewing whether a new investment fund is needed beyond 2027/28.
findings.matters: Suggests the council identified deliverability or risk constraints within its investment program; signals uncertainty about future investment strategy post-2026/27.
findings.figures: 2026/27 is final year for WIF commitments
findings.quote: The WIF strategy includes proposals to reduce the overall level of investment, coming into the final year of the fund in 2026/27. This ensures that the level of planned activity is deliverable and that it is within an acceptable level of risk.

findings.paper_title: Revised Treasury Management Strategy and Investment Strategy Report
findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision policy updated to Asset Life method
findings.detail: The council has updated its MRP policy for 2026/27 to use the Asset Life (Equal Instalment) Method for both existing and new borrowing, ensuring sufficient resources are provisioned to fully repay all borrowing over a prudent period.
findings.matters: Changes how the council provisions for debt repayment; affects cash reserves drawdown rate and debt servicing patterns.
findings.figures: Policy change effective 2026/27
findings.quote: The new policy adopts the Asset Life (Equal Instalment) Method for both existing and new borrowing, ensuring that sufficient resources are set aside to fully repay both external and internal borrowing over a prudent period and aligns with statutory guidance.

findings.paper_title: Revised Treasury Management Strategy and Investment Strategy Report
findings.headline: Debt maturity concentration 2050-2060 creates refinancing risk
findings.detail: The council's existing debt profile includes a significant concentration due to be repaid between 2050-2060. When new borrowing is taken, the council plans to spread maturities more evenly to mitigate exposure to interest rate volatility.
findings.matters: Concentrated debt maturity creates structural refinancing risk and exposure to interest rate volatility; future borrowing decisions must account for this imbalance.
findings.figures: Debt concentration: 2050-2060
findings.quote: The current borrowing maturity profile includes a concentration of debt due to be repaid around 2050-2060 (Appendix 2 Annex 2). When new borrowing is taken out the opportunity will be taken to consider spreading out the maturity profile more evenly as doing this mitigates exposure to interest rate volatility.

findings.paper_title: Revised Treasury Management Strategy and Investment Strategy Report
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement forecast to increase
findings.detail: The need to borrow (CFR) is expected to increase as a result of the council's capital strategy, specifically driven by investments in the Warwickshire Property Development Group and Warwickshire Investment Fund.
findings.matters: Signals increasing debt issuance and leverage over the medium term, affecting the council's balance sheet and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Specific CFR projections in Appendix 2, Table 4 (not visible in main text)
findings.quote: The need to borrow, also referred to as the Capital Financing Requirement or CFR (Appendix 2, Table 4), is forecast to increase. This increase is driven by the planned capital strategy, including investments in WPDG and the WIF.

findings.paper_title: Revised Treasury Management Strategy and Investment Strategy Report
findings.headline: External borrowing required from 2027/28 as DSG grant boost ends
findings.detail: The council is currently managing through internal borrowing and the DSG High Needs Stability Grant (received autumn 2026), but once cash balances decline from 2027/28, new external borrowing will be required to maintain liquidity and meet operational needs. This marks a shift from current cash-based management to market access dependency within 24 months.
findings.matters: Indicates the council will need to access capital markets within two years; affects refinancing risk exposure and borrowing costs.
findings.figures: DSG High Needs Stability Grant autumn 2026; external borrowing required 2027/28 onwards
findings.quote: As cash balances decline from 2027/28, new external borrowing is expected to be required to maintain liquidity and meet operational requirements.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Capital Strategy 2026-31 (17.02.26)
findings.headline: Percentage of revenue budget committed to capital financing costs increasing due to borrowing expansion
findings.detail: The council notes that the percentage of its revenue budget committed to capital financing costs is increasing in the long term due to expansion of the capital programme through the Capital Investment Fund, creation of Warwickshire Property and Development Group and Warwickshire Investment Fund, and need to manage cumulative DSG overspend. This reduces revenue flexibility for service delivery.
findings.matters: This directly affects the council's ability to maintain service quality or respond to pressures. Growing capital financing commitments can crowd out revenue spending on services. Finance directors and lenders both care about this inflexibility.
findings.figures: 71% increase in total revenue cost of borrowing by 2030/31
findings.quote: The percentage of the Council's revenue budget that is committed to capital financing costs is increasing in the long term due to the expansion of the capital programme through the Capital Investment Fund, the creation of Warwickshire Property and Development Group and the Warwickshire Investment Fund, and the need to manage the cashflow impact of the cumulative DSG overspend.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Capital Strategy 2026-31 (17.02.26)
findings.headline: Capital Investment Fund pipeline will exceed available resources; prioritisation critical
findings.detail: The council has established a Capital Investment Fund funded by borrowing from which services bid for capital allocations. The strategy explicitly states there is a high probability that the emerging pipeline of projects will exceed available CIF resources over the MTFS period. This creates a prioritisation challenge. The council has set annual borrowing allocations for the CIF that are subject to Full Council approval, but the underlying demand exceeds what can be funded.
findings.matters: This signals constrained capital resources relative to demand. The council will face hard choices about which investments to defer or cancel. The strategic significance is that despite substantial planned borrowing, capacity remains limited.
findings.figures: Pipeline exceeds available CIF resources over MTFS period
findings.quote: A pipeline of potential projects underpinning these areas of focus has been provided by services and will continue to be monitored and amended by the Capital Strategy Group. However, there is a high probability that the emerging pipeline will exceed the available CIF resources over the MTFS period, therefore, prioritisation of which schemes the Council invests is very important.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Capital Strategy 2026-31 (17.02.26)
findings.headline: Aging population will create £186m DSG-related pressures and increased social care demand by 2035
findings.detail: Those aged 70+ projected to increase by 9.5% and 85+ by 27.1% between 2026-2031. By end of decade, 4,935 residents in care homes aged 65+, a 35.7% increase from 2025. Dementia rates predicted to increase by 29.6% in 65+ age group between 2025-2035. The council is expanding children's homes and developing extra care and specialised supported housing, but services may require further capital investment for accommodation-based provision.
findings.matters: Demographic change is driving service demand that the council cannot reduce. The strategic link is that this population growth also creates the DSG deficit (rising High Needs block demand) and capital pressures for new accommodation. This is a structural, long-term cost driver.
findings.figures: 70+ increase by 9.5%; 85+ increase by 27.1%; 4,935 residents in care homes (35.7% increase); dementia increase of 29.6%
findings.quote: By the end of the decade there will be an estimated 4,935 residents in care homes aged over 65, which represents a 35.7% increase from the 2025 estimate. Dementia represents the biggest growing cause of disability and rates are predicted to increase by 29.6% in people aged 65 or over in Warwickshire between 2025-2035.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Capital Strategy 2026-31 (17.02.26)
findings.headline: Forward funding of developer contributions is capped at £30m exposure due to cash flow risk
findings.detail: The council is using forward funding—borrowing upfront for infrastructure like school expansions before developer contributions arrive—to bridge timing gaps. This creates cash flow risk if developers delay or fail to pay. The council has explicitly set an upper limit of £30m exposure at any point to limit aggregate risk across multiple forward-funded schemes, citing concern about DSG deficits already putting significant pressure on cash balances.
findings.matters: This reveals the council is already under cash pressure and managing liquidity risk carefully. Forward funding can amplify vulnerability to market downturns or housing market slowdowns that delay developer payments.
findings.figures: £30m exposure limit
findings.quote: Due to the increased risk this approach introduces, the wider capital funding issues and SEND deficits putting significant pressure on cash balances, an upper limit on forward funding of £30m exposure at any point will be applied to ensure the aggregate risk to the council of numerous forward funded schemes is limited.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Capital Strategy 2026-31 (17.02.26)
findings.headline: DSG deficit is forcing £186m of the planned £243m debt increase
findings.detail: Of the planned £243m increase in external debt over the MTFS period, £186m is attributed to the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit through end of 2027/28. The government provided funding for 90% of the High Needs Block deficit up to end of 2025/26, but this is a structural problem. The council notes it is likely further High Needs Stability Grants will be provided for 2026/27 and 2027/28 but acknowledges uncertainty about future years' grant levels.
findings.matters: This reveals a significant structural pressure on the council's finances that is outside the council's direct control. Borrowing to cover a grants shortfall is different from borrowing for capital investment. This dependency on future discretionary government grants is a risk factor.
findings.figures: £186 million can be attributed to the DSG deficit to the end of 2027/28; Of the £243 million increase in the external debt balance over the MTFS period
findings.quote: Of the £243 million increase in the external debt balance over the MTFS period, £186 million can be attributed to the DSG deficit to the end of 2027/28 after allowing for the government's announcement in February 2026 that funding will be provided for 90% of the High Needs Block deficit up to the end of 2025/26. It is likely that further High Needs Stability Grants will be provided for 2026/27 and 2027/28

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Capital Strategy 2026-31 (17.02.26)
findings.headline: Planned borrowing of £261m by 2030/31 will increase revenue financing costs by 71%
findings.detail: The council is planning substantial new borrowing to fund its capital programme. New borrowing rises from £184m in 2027/28 to £261m by 2030/31. The revenue cost of servicing this borrowing—including interest and Minimum Revenue Provision—is forecast to increase from around £23m in 2026/27 to £45m by 2030/31, a 71% increase. This growing commitment eats into the revenue budget available for service delivery.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that the council can sustainably service this increasing debt burden. Finance directors need visibility of the growing strain on the revenue budget from capital financing costs.
findings.figures: New borrowing of £184 million in 2027/28 increasing to £261 million of new borrowing by the end of 2030/31; total revenue cost of past and planned new borrowing will increase by 71% over the period of the 2026-31 Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.quote: New borrowing of £184 million in 2027/28 increasing to £261 million of new borrowing by the end of 2030/31, is affordable within the 2026-31 Medium Term Financial Strategy and is deemed to be the minimum level of borrowing needed over the medium term to support the delivery of Council Plan objectives.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and 2026-31 Medium Term Financial Strategy (Covering Report)
findings.headline: Cascading delays to district and borough council budget processes pending Warwickshire precept
findings.detail: Some Warwickshire district and borough councils have postponed their own budget meetings because Warwickshire County Council did not agree its budget on 5 February. The precept must be issued by 1 March so that district councils can prepare and issue consolidated council tax bills; the delay cascades across the local authority ecosystem.
findings.matters: Budget impasse extends beyond the council itself and affects other authorities' ability to operate and issue bills; signals governance dysfunction with wider system impact.
findings.figures: Not specified in paper
findings.quote: We are aware that some Warwickshire district and borough councils have postponed planned budget meetings as a result of the Council not agreeing a budget on 5 February.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and 2026-31 Medium Term Financial Strategy (Covering Report)
findings.headline: High Needs Stability Grant of £7.1m received late in final finance settlement and incorporated into budget proposals
findings.detail: Final Local Government Finance Settlement released 9 February 2026 announced the High Needs Stability Grant, which was incorporated into the budget as a £7.1m revenue budget benefit. This late-arriving funding materially changed the budget propositions between the adjourned meeting and this reconvened one.
findings.matters: Material late-arriving funding (£7.1m) to a council in budget difficulty; lender should understand how dependent the agreed position is on this grant.
findings.figures: £7.1m revenue budget benefit
findings.quote: Addition of the £7.1m revenue budget benefit from the High Needs Stability Grant within the Budget Reductions

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and 2026-31 Medium Term Financial Strategy (Covering Report)
findings.headline: Section 114 notice from Chief Finance Officer becomes likely if budget not agreed on this attempt
findings.detail: The paper sets out that if budget remains unagreed, the section 151 officer would be forced to consider issuing a Section 114 notice because the council's expenditure would likely exceed its resources. This immediately restricts new spending commitments and triggers government intervention.
findings.matters: Section 114 is a formal declaration that spending exceeds resources—a high-intervention trigger that restricts council operations and signals financial control failure.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this paper
findings.quote: the section 151 officer (the Chief Finance Officer) would be forced to consider issuing a section 114 notice under section 114 of the Local Government Finance Act 1988 as the Council's expenditure would likely exceed its resources; this would immediately restrict new spending commitments and could lead to Government intervention

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and 2026-31 Medium Term Financial Strategy (Covering Report)
findings.headline: Council adjourned budget meeting on 5 February without reaching agreement; reconvening 17 February under Section 114 threat
findings.detail: The scheduled budget meeting on 5 February adjourned without the council agreeing a budget. This meeting on 17 February is the continuation. If agreement is still not reached, the meeting will be adjourned again but must reconvene before end of February to meet the 1 March precept deadline. The covering report explicitly flags that if no budget is agreed, the Chief Finance Officer would be forced to consider issuing a Section 114 notice because the council's expenditure would likely exceed its resources.
findings.matters: A council unable to agree its budget on first attempt signals governance friction and immediate financial control risks; Section 114 notice would restrict all new spending and trigger government intervention.
findings.figures: Statutory deadline 1 March 2026
findings.quote: Council met on 5 February, and the meeting adjourned without a budget having been agreed; this meeting is a continuation of the adjourned meeting.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Annual Governance Statement 2024/25
findings.headline: Sickness absence increased during the year and is now stabilising, driven by stress and mental health
findings.detail: The council reports sickness absence has increased in line with national benchmarks and is only now beginning to stabilise. Stress and mental health are identified as the highest causes. This workforce issue will likely increase employer costs and may reduce service delivery capacity when combined with ongoing budget pressures.
findings.matters: Elevated sickness absence reduces the council's ability to deliver savings or manage unexpected cost pressures. It is also a leading indicator of employee dissatisfaction and potential further workforce deterioration.
findings.figures: Sickness absence has increased and then stabilised; stress and mental health the highest cause
findings.quote: In line with national benchmarks, sickness absence rates have increased and then started to stabilise in the last year, with stress and mental health being the highest [categories].

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Annual Governance Statement 2024/25
findings.headline: Warwickshire Investment Fund Business Investment Growth pillar closed due to insufficient demand
findings.detail: The council reshaped its investment strategy in 2024/25, closing the bulk of the Business Investment Growth pillar of the Warwickshire Investment Fund because demand was insufficient. Other pillars remain active. This represents a contraction in the council's appetite or capacity for commercial returns.
findings.matters: A council reducing commercial investment activity may indicate reduced confidence in the investment environment or need to preserve liquidity. Combined with service pressures, it suggests financial caution.
findings.figures: Bulk of Business Investment Growth pillar closed
findings.quote: In the 2024/25 Investment Strategy, the Warwickshire Investment Fund was reshaped. This included closing the bulk of the Business Investment Growth pillar of the Fund as demand was not sufficient.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Annual Governance Statement 2024/25
findings.headline: Governance over SEND and social care budgets tightened due to financial pressures
findings.detail: In response to heightened financial challenges in SEND, home-to-school transport and social care, the council created an 'executive-led Budget Delivery Oversight Group' to increase scrutiny of budgets, governance around expenditure, and delivery of proposed savings. This governance escalation signals the council recognises these areas as out of control and requiring intervention.
findings.matters: When a council creates new oversight structures for specific services, it signals those services are not tracking to plan. This is a leading indicator of reserve drawdown or unmet savings.
findings.figures: New executive-led oversight group created
findings.quote: Reflecting the heightened financial challenges around key services including Special Educational Needs and Disabilities, home to school transport, and Social Care, the Council has strengthened budget oversight with the formation of an executive-led Budget Delivery Oversight Group to increase scrutiny around budgets for those areas, governance around associated expenditure, and the delivery of proposed savings.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Annual Governance Statement 2024/25
findings.headline: SEND, home-to-school transport, and social care have emerged as the most significant service funding challenges
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies SEND (including inclusion services), home-to-school transport, and adults/children's social care as the areas facing the most significant funding pressures. These are demand-driven services where the council has limited ability to reduce demand. The pressure is material enough that the council formed a new executive-led Budget Delivery Oversight Group specifically to increase scrutiny of budgets and savings delivery in these areas.
findings.matters: These three areas represent structural cost pressures that grow faster than general inflation. A lender tracking council solvency needs to know which service areas are creating unfunded cost pressures.
findings.figures: Budget Delivery Oversight Group formed for heightened oversight of these specific services
findings.quote: The most significant areas of challenge have included funding pressures in the areas of Special Educational Needs and Disability (SEND) and Inclusion services, home to school transport provision, an increased need for school places and the provision of Adults and Children's Social Care services.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Annual Governance Statement 2024/25
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit is now a new strategic risk for financial resilience
findings.detail: The council added a new strategic risk specifically in Q4 2024/25 regarding the Dedicated Schools Grant. The risk is scored at 16 against a target of 12, directly flagging financial resilience concerns. This reflects the growing cumulative deficit in the DSG, which is a statutory pressure councils cannot pass to schools.
findings.matters: DSG deficits represent an unfunded liability that eventually crystallises in the general fund. A lender needs to know when a council recognises this as a strategic risk to financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Strategic risk score 16, target 12

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - External Auditors' Annual Audit Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Auditors identified a significant weakness in DSG deficit management and raised a key recommendation requiring continued enhanced monitoring and treasury oversight.
findings.detail: Auditors assessed that despite the council having governance, monitoring, and mitigation arrangements in place, overall funding has not been adequate to reduce the growth of the deficit. The council is implementing mitigations (increasing resourced provision places, piloting Inclusion Framework, workforce development) but the number of EHCPs and unit costs continue to rise. Auditors raised a key recommendation for continued delivery of planned mitigations and enhanced cashflow and treasury monitoring due to immediate impact on cash position.
findings.matters: An audit key recommendation signals significant weakness identified by external auditors in a core financial sustainability arrangement, requiring active management and monitoring by the council's finance team and audit committee.
findings.figures: Number of EHCPs and unit costs continuing to rise despite mitigation efforts
findings.quote: The Council should continue to deliver its planned mitigations and current governance arrangements of monitoring and reporting on deficit within established processes. Due to the immediate impact on cash flow the Council should continue to implement enhanced cashflow and treasury monitoring.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - External Auditors' Annual Audit Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Council recently moved to 'no overall control' governance following May 2025 elections, with Reform UK as largest party.
findings.detail: Following May 2025 elections, the council moved from its previous governance model to 'no overall control' with Reform UK as the largest party providing the council leader. This represents a significant political change that may affect budget priorities, decision-making speed, and implementation of planned strategies.
findings.matters: A lender should understand that a change in political control during a period of financial pressure (DSG deficit, savings targets) may affect the council's capacity to deliver planned financial recovery and mitigation actions.
findings.figures: Elections held May 2025; Council now under 'no overall control'
findings.quote: The most recent elections were in May 2025 since when the Council have been under 'no overall control' with Reform UK being the largest party and providing the leader of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - External Auditors' Annual Audit Report 2024/25
findings.headline: 2024/25 budget overspend of £1.983m driven by social care and children's services cost increases, partially offset by strong treasury performance.
findings.detail: The council overspent by £1.983m (0.49% above budget) in 2024/25, with increases in Social Care, Children and Families, and Environment services. A financial recovery plan implemented at Q1 when forecast overspend reached £27m reduced the outturn gap but did not eliminate it. The council remained within its 2% target margin. Strong treasury performance and investment returns helped mitigate the overspend.
findings.matters: Persistent cost pressures in social care and children's services are sector-wide but the council's experience shows they are not yet stabilized within the budget envelope, requiring ongoing financial discipline.
findings.figures: £1.983m overspend (0.49% of budget); initially forecast £27m overspend at Q1; forecast overspend reduced by approximately £12m through recovery plan; achieved within 2% target margin
findings.quote: The Council concluded the 2024/25 financial year with an overspend of £1.983 million, or 0.49% above budget, largely due to increased costs in Social Care, Children and Families, and Environment services.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - External Auditors' Annual Audit Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Council delivered only 61% of 2024/25 savings target and faces ongoing challenge meeting £21.8m savings requirement for 2025/26.
findings.detail: The council achieved only 61% of its savings target in 2024/25, largely due to higher than anticipated costs in young people's residential care and other service shortfalls. For 2025/26, the council expects to achieve 91% of its savings target with £21.8m in savings planned, and £79.6m savings required by March 2030. This pattern of underperformance against savings plans combined with escalating demand pressures in high-cost areas suggests implementation risk.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can consistently deliver on savings plans that are central to balancing budgets, particularly given prior-year miss and increasing structural pressures in social care and education.
findings.figures: 61% of 2024/25 savings target achieved; £21.8m savings target for 2025/26; £79.6m total savings target by March 2030; 91% of 2025/26 target expected to be achieved
findings.quote: While the Council has met most of its savings goals in the past, it achieved only 61% of its target in 2024/25, largely due to higher than anticipated costs in young people's residential care and other service shortfalls. For 2025/26, the Council expects to achieve 91% of its savings target.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - External Auditors' Annual Audit Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block deficit forecast to reach £146.2m by March 2026, exceeding 34% of useable reserves and creating material long-term financial risk.
findings.detail: The cumulative DSG deficit stood at £77.9m at 31 March 2025 and is forecast to rise to £143.8m by March 2026 and exceed £300m by March 2028. The council relies on a statutory override to defer impact to the general fund, but this expires in March 2028. Without national policy change or significant local delivery shifts, the council may need to absorb the deficit within its general fund, severely compromising financial resilience and forcing use of reserves earmarked for other priorities.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director needs to understand that 34% of the council's useable reserves are already committed to covering an unfunded statutory obligation that is growing faster than any planned mitigation can address, leaving limited financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £77.9m cumulative deficit at 31 March 2025; forecast £143.8m by March 2026; forecast to exceed £300m by March 2028; deficit equivalent to 34% of total useable reserves; £44.7m of 2024/25 in-year deficit not covered by reserves
findings.quote: At 31 March 2025, the cumulative DSG deficit stood at £77.9 million, equivalent to 34% of the Council's total useable reserves. The deficit is forecast to rise to £143.8 million by March 2026 and exceed £300 million by March 2028.

findings.paper_title: Annual Update to Strategic Risk Management Framework
findings.headline: Risk appetite for workforce escalated to 'Cautious' over concern about loss of critical officers
findings.detail: The council has escalated its risk appetite for People (Workforce) and staff health and wellbeing from more open/minimalist positions to 'Cautious'. This signals heightened concern about the risk of losing critical officers, though the paper does not detail the underlying drivers or current staffing situation.
findings.matters: Loss or instability of critical finance or senior officers could impair the council's financial management capacity and service delivery, particularly during anticipated Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: People (Workforce i.e. risk of loss of critical officers) and the wider category area of staff health and well-being were both adjusted to "Cautious" from open and minimalist respectively.
